prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**The Court May Consider [the Document] Without Converting Defendant's Motion into One for Summary Judgment.**

A court deciding a Rule 12(b)(6) motion must consider the complaint in its entirety, including "documents incorporated into the complaint by reference." *Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd.*, 551 U.S. 308, 322 (2007). Rule 12(d) requires conversion when "matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d). An incorporated document is not such a matter. It is treated as part of the pleading itself. *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 907–08 (9th Cir. 2003). A court may therefore consider it "without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment." *Id.* at 908.

**A. Ninth Circuit law reaches documents on which the complaint relies.**

A plaintiff cannot keep a document out of the Rule 12(b)(6) record simply by declining to attach it. "[D]ocuments whose contents are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no party questions, but which are not physically attached to the pleading, may be considered in ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss." *Branch v. Tunnell*, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994), *overruled on other grounds by* *Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119 (9th Cir. 2002). Incorporation is proper "if the plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908. Relatedly, a court may consider material on which the complaint necessarily relies when (1) the complaint refers to the document, (2) the document is central to the plaintiff's claim, and (3) no party questions the authenticity of the copy attached to the motion. *Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006) (considering a release on a motion to dismiss).

The doctrine also reaches documents the complaint does not expressly describe. When the plaintiff's claim depends on a document's contents, the defendant attaches it to the motion, and its authenticity is undisputed, the court may consider it even though the plaintiff does not explicitly allege those contents. *Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076–77 (9th Cir. 2005) (considering web pages surrounding an allegedly defamatory photograph and caption); *see Parrino v. FHP, Inc.*, 146 F.3d 699, 705–06 (9th Cir. 1998) (considering health plan documents on which the claims depended), *superseded by statute on other grounds as stated in* *Abrego Abrego v. Dow Chemical Co.*, 443 F.3d 676 (9th Cir. 2006).

**B. The doctrine prevents selective pleading.**

Incorporation by reference "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018). Once a document is incorporated, the court "may assume that its contents are true for purposes of a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6)." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908. Nor must the court accept allegations that contradict documents properly before it. *See Daniels-Hall v. National Education Ass'n*, 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010) (court need not accept as true allegations contradicting attached exhibits or judicially noticeable matters).

The doctrine has limits. A passing mention of a document is not enough. *Coto Settlement v. Eisenberg*, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010). And a court may not assume an incorporated document's truth solely to dispute well-pleaded factual allegations. *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1003. Defendant's request respects both limits.

**C. [The Document] is properly before the Court.**

The Complaint [refers extensively to / quotes] [the Document]. *See* Compl. ¶¶ [__]. [The Document] also forms the basis of Plaintiff's [claim], because Plaintiff cannot establish [element] without relying on its terms. *See id.* ¶¶ [__]. A true and correct copy is attached as Exhibit [__], and its authenticity is not subject to reasonable question. Defendant offers it to show what it says, namely [identify provision], not to resolve any genuine factual dispute. The Court should consider [the Document] in its entirety and decide this motion under Rule 12(b)(6), without converting it into a motion for summary judgment.
